source_says: Aug. 1691: Kelsey, travelling with Assiniboins, comes 40 miles beyond the buffalo to “the Mountain Poets, the Hill Stoneys, i.e. Assiniboins, probably of the Touchwood Hills” (place Morton’s)
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), pp. 112–13

source_says: Aug. 1691: the Naywatame Poets, reached northward from the Touchwood Hills “in the direction of Nipawi”; “these should be the Gros Ventres, the Fall or Rapid Indians” (identification Morton’s)
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 113

source_says: Winter 1691–92: Kelsey spends “the winter on the prairies north-east of Saskatoon, hunting buffalo” with his Assiniboins
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 113

source_says: Mooney estimated “there must have been 7,000 Comanche about 1690”
source: Mooney (1928), as given in Swanton, Indian Tribes of North America, p. 314

source_says: Knife River villages: “the Big Hidatsa village was established around 1600”; Awatixa Xi’e the oldest of the three
source: Wikipedia, “Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Northern Arapaho tradition (1892) of the Kiowa at the Three Forks of the Missouri, applied to the Plains Apache only on the assumption that they were already with the Kiowa (kept off the division track)
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), pp. 155–56

source_says: Northern Arapaho tradition (1892): when they first knew the Kiowa, the Kiowa “lived about the Three forks of the Missouri”; date ours (“probably about or before 1700”)
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), pp. 155–56

source_says: Opler: “a judicious estimate of all Lipan Apache in 1700, including those living in Mexico, would be about 6,000”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Opler, “Lipan Apache”, p. 945

source_says: The great Dakota village of Kathio (Izatys) at Mille Lacs, the source of the Rum River; Du Lhut counted “40 Sioux villages in the vicinity” in 1679
source: Wikipedia, “Battle of Kathio” (site coordinates and participants) (belligerent: Mdewakanton Dakota)

source_says: By 1690–1700 the Shoshone “were probably already established in the Missouri Basin”; little sign of them north of the Missouri (Binnema’s reconstruction)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 84

source_says: 1700: the name first recorded, when Governor Rodríguez Cubero has a condemned man’s head set on a pole at Taos to warn the “apaches de la xicarilla” (their mountains northeast of Taos; place ours)
source: Ortiz, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 10: Southwest (1983), Tiller, “Jicarilla Apache”, p. 449

source_says: “In 1700 they were, according to Le Sueur, on Blue Earth River near the Iowa”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Winter 1700–01: 60 lodges of Wahpekute Santee winter at Le Sueur’s Fort L’Huillier
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 726

source_says: Winter 1700–01: 150 lodges of Yankton winter with Le Sueur at Fort L’Huillier on the Blue Earth River; in May 1701, 200 lodges camp near the fort
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 726

source_says: 1701: the Iowa join the tribes gathering at Fort L’Huillier on the Blue Earth River, then flee west again
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 434

source_says: Iberville, 1702: 1,500
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, p. 472, table 2

source_says: Iberville (1702): 2,000 “Panas” families, “a population in excess of 10,000, assuming a minimum of five individuals in a family” (Parks)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 563

source_says: Le Sueur, 1702: the Sioux number 4,000 families
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 748

source_says: Ulibarrí, leaving Taos on 20 July 1706, meets “several friendly Apache bands, probably Jicarilla” on “the upper courses of the Canadian and Cimarron rivers” (identification probable; centre ours)
source: Wikipedia, “Juan de Ulibarrí” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Ulibarrí at El Cuartelejo, “the main village… on Ladder Creek”, 1706; at least five Cuartelejo rancherías
source: Wikipedia, “El Cuartelejo” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: After leaving Fort L’Huillier the Iowa “may have chosen to live along the Little Sioux River below Spirit and Okoboji lakes” (date ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 434

source_says: Lehmer: of more than 60 Arikara village sites, perhaps 22 occupied at once, at 40 houses and 10 to a household: 8,800 for the early 18th century
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, pp. 246–48, table 1

source_says: Lehmer: villages provisionally Hidatsa, about 1675–1750, hold over 640 houses; at Thompson’s 13 to a household, “over 8,300”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, pp. 246–48, table 1

source_says: Lehmer: six sites between Square Buttes and the Heart River, about 1675–1750, with some 620 houses: a Mandan population “of over 8,000”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, pp. 246–48, table 1

source_says: Bourgmont: three Arikara villages on the west bank of the Missouri above the Niobrara, and 40 villages farther upriver on both banks (kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Arikara”, p. 366

source_says: Bourgmont lives at “the Missouria village at the mouth of the Grand River”, from 1712
source: Wikipedia, “Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont” (site coordinates and participants); Wikipedia, “Fort Orleans” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Bourgmont, about 1714: the Otoe at a village on Salt Creek about 10 leagues from the mouth of the Platte; no Otoe villages east of the Missouri after this
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 447

source_says: Before about 1730 the Jicarilla and Carlana, “close relatives” of the Cuartelejo and Paloma, “lived in fixed villages along the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains” (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Gunnerson, “Plains Village Tradition: Western Periphery”, p. 244

source_says: Vermale’s map of 1717 shows 10 Padouca villages north of the Pawnee villages; earlier maps had put the Plains Apacheans south of the Pawnee (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Foster and McCollough, “Plains Apache”, p. 928

source_says: 1718: Bienville lists a Kitsai group living with several Caddo groups in a single village 150 leagues up the Red River (place ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 567

source_says: Lehmer: “a conservative estimate for the year 1719 is 15,000, based on historical sources” (the Wichita “and closely related groups”)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, p. 247

source_says: 1719: du Rivage, 70 leagues up the Red River near present Paris, Texas, meets warriors of five groups, among them Tonkawa and Yojuane, returning from an attack on Apaches farther west (a war party; kept off the track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb and Campbell, “Tonkawa”, p. 954; DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 567

source_says: Lasley Vore site on the Arkansas in Tulsa County: “a Wichita village of about 6,000 people, as described by… La Harpe” in 1719
source: Wikipedia, “Lasley Vore Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Du Tisné finds “two likely Taovaya villages… near the present-day Neodesha, Kansas”, 1719
source: Wikipedia, “Taovaya” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Du Tisné’s two Taovaya villages near Neodesha, 130 grass houses and 200–250 warriors each: between them 2,080–2,600 people (the Taovaya only; a partial count)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, pp. 550, 561

source_says: David Thompson, in 1787, found that the testimony of elderly Piegan ... clearly pointed to that tribe's residence on the Saskatchewan Plains, near the Eagle Hills, some 400 miles east of the Rockies, in the early 18th century.
source: Ewers, The Horse in Blackfoot Indian Culture (BAE Bulletin 159, 1955), p. 300 (pdf 324)

source_says: The Villasur expedition passes through El Cuartelejo, 1720
source: Wikipedia, “El Cuartelejo” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Pawnee and Otoe attack Villasur’s camp just south of the Loup–Platte confluence near Columbus, 14 Aug. 1720
source: Wikipedia, “Villasur expedition” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Pawnee and Otoe attack Villasur’s camp at the Loup–Platte confluence, 14 Aug. 1720 (the Loup villages were the Skiri’s; division ours)
source: Wikipedia, “Villasur expedition” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Renaudière: a Pawnee village of 150 lodges 15 leagues up the Loup, and eight more villages farther upriver about half a league apart
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, pp. 517–18

source_says: Fort Orleans built beside the Missouria village near the mouth of the Grand River, Nov. 1723
source: Wikipedia, “Fort Orleans” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Bourgmont reaches “the main Kaw village on the Missouri near Doniphan” on 8 July 1724: “a large settlement, with at least 1,500 persons”
source: Wikipedia, “Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: July 1724: Bourgmont finds the principal Kansa village on the west bank of the Missouri north of Independence Creek, Doniphan County
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, pp. 462–63

source_says: Bourgmont reaches the Padouca (Apache) village on the upper Little Arkansas, probably near Lyons, 18 Oct. 1724: 140 dwellings, “about 800 men, more than 1,500 women, and about 2,000 children”; the chief claimed twelve villages
source: Wikipedia, “Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Saukamappee’s youth (about 1730): “a large camp of the Snake Indians on the Plains of the Eagle Hill”; date from his age, place from Thompson’s gloss; a war-season camp at the northern reach of Shoshone raiding, dated only by the narrator’s age (kept off the division track, which would otherwise put the Shoshone north of every Blackfoot division)
source: David Thompson’s Narrative of His Explorations in Western America, 1784–1812, ed. Tyrrell (Champlain Society, 1916), pp. 328–29

source_says: 1733: a mission founded for the Jicarilla five leagues north of Taos; the governor soon drives them back into the mountains
source: Ortiz, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 10: Southwest (1983), Tiller, “Jicarilla Apache”, p. 450

source_says: After six hours they found them encamped to the number of 60 Assiniboin, 30 of their wives, and 10 Cree, awaiting my reply. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 144 (pdf 178), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Report of La Vérendrye (undated)

source_says: “Around 1734 the Omaha established their first village west of the Missouri River on Bow Creek in present-day Cedar County, Nebraska”
source: Wikipedia, “Omaha people” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Biesterfeldt site on the Sheyenne River near Lisbon, North Dakota: “an independent group of Cheyennes is believed to have occupied it c. 1724–1780”
source: Wikipedia, “Biesterfeldt Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: My cousin La Vérendrye has written to me to say that he had seen three hundred cabins of Assiniboin and that he would have seen a great many more if he had had a supply of goods. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 199 (pdf 235), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): La Jemeraye to Beauharnois, 23 July 1735

source_says: M.H. Wright: about 8,000 in 1736
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Opler, “Lipan Apache”, p. 945

source_says: 1736: 300 Sioux men east of the Mississippi and 2,000 on the prairies
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 722

source_says: Eight hundred Cree and Assiniboin already assembled at Pointe du Bois fort are awaiting us. (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 228 (pdf 264), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Report of La Vérendrye (headed 2 June 1736; journal to 173

source_says: On the sixteenth La Colle’s man who passed by the Assiniboin said that the two tribes are at present hunting buffalo to get meat and fats for the fort ; some of them return laden every day. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 240 (pdf 276), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Report of La Vérendrye (headed 2 June 1736; journal to 173

source_says: there were seventy of their people and fifty Cree a day’s journey away laden with meat and fats to escort me. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 241 (pdf 277), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Report of La Vérendrye (headed 2 June 1736; journal to 173

source_says: time was required to notify two villages of the Assiniboin situated at the great fork of the Red river (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 244 (pdf 280), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Report of La Vérendrye (headed 2 June 1736; journal to 173

source_says: I enquired of the Assiniboin where they meant to spend the summer ; and they said that on returning from the war they would go to the country of the Koüathéattes to buy Indian corn and beans (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 253 (pdf 289), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Report of La Vérendrye (headed 2 June 1736; journal to 173

source_says: the Assiniboin to the number of eight hundred had left at the end of April to go and take vengeance on the Sioux for the Frenchmen [they had killed], and that the Cree and the Monsoni had also raised war parties ... but that small-pox having broken out among them they were obliged to stop (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 282 (pdf 318), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Beauharnois to Maurepas, 1 Oct. 1738

source_says: I proceeded to the fork of the Assiniboine and, reaching there on the 24th, I found ten cabins of Cree, including two war chiefs, awaiting me with a large quantity of meat (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 298 (pdf 336), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: On the third day after our departure an Assiniboin village of forty lodges joined us with the object of speaking to me. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 311 (pdf 349), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: La Vérendrye, from Fort La Reine (Oct. 1738): “Joining a large band of Assiniboines, he pushed southwest across the prairie” to the Mandan
source: Wikipedia, “Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: To crown our luck he took us twenty-two leagues out of our way to visit a village of a hundred and two lodges that he had gone to discover (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 313 (pdf 351), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: We left on the morning of the 30th, about 600 men and several women without children, some of the best walkers. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 324 (pdf 362), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: I gave orders to count the cabins, and we found that there were about one hundred and thirty. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 339 (pdf 377), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: We remarked that in the plain there are several small forts of from forty to fifty cabins each, constructed in the same manner as the large ones. At present they are uninhabited. We were given to understand that they went there in summer in order to work in the fields (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 346 (pdf 384), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: On the 22nd of the present month I learnt from a savage that a large band of Assiniboin had gathered at the Lake of the Prairies, and are making canoes in order to go to the English. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 358 (pdf 396), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: ascended it as far as the fork, which is the rendezvous every spring of the Cree of the Mountains, Prairies, and Rivers to deliberate as to what they shall do— go and trade with the French or with the English. (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 487 (pdf 527), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Mémorandum respecting the map [1749]

source_says: On the same day, the 10th, in the evening fifteen Assiniboin came to tell us that they belonged to a band of sixty lodges ... They came on the 18th and did their trading in a short time. (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 359 (pdf 397), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of La Vérendrye, 20 July 1738–May 1739

source_says: The Mallet brothers visit the Panimaha (Skiri) at the mouth of the Loup, 1739
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: 1739 or 1740: the French build Fort de Cavagnial next to the Kansa village, then near the mouth of Salt Creek
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, p. 463

source_says: fort Dauphin, the fifth establishment, made at the request of the Cree of the Prairies and the Canoe Assiniboin. (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 485 (pdf 525), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Mémorandum respecting the map [1749]

source_says: I established a new fort at the request of the mountain Cree on the Lake of the Prairies last autumn, and named it fort Dauphin. (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 378 (pdf 416), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): La Vérendrye to Maurepas, 12 May 1742

source_says: Being near the main village of the Gens du Serpent our scouts came to inform us that they had all made their escape with great precipitation, and that they had abandoned their lodges and a large part of their effects. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 420 (pdf 458), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of the Chevalier de la Vérendrye, 1742–43

source_says: On the 15th of March we arrived among the Gens de la Petite Cerise. They were returning from their winter quarters, and were two days’ march from their fort, which is on the bank of the Missouri. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 425 (pdf 463), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of the Chevalier de la Vérendrye, 1742–43

source_says: “An Arikara village, near where present-day Pierre, South Dakota developed, was visited in 1743 by two sons of… La Vérendrye”
source: Wikipedia, “Arikara” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: We passed by fort La Butte on the morning of the 27th, but the Assiniboin had just left. ... We hastened our march somewhat and caught up with the Assiniboin at their encampment. There were over a hundred of them and we continued our route together. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 430 (pdf 468), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of the Chevalier de la Vérendrye, 1742–43

source_says: We reached the village near the mountain on the 2nd of June. As our horses were tired we suspended our journey and remained in the village till the 20th. (place ours) (part)
source: Burpee, ed., Journals and Letters of Pierre Gaultier de Varennes de la Vérendrye and His Sons (1927), p. 431 (pdf 469), La Vérendrye (Burpee ed. 1927): Journal of the Chevalier de la Vérendrye, 1742–43

source_says: Mille Lacs, before the Ojibwe destroyed Kathio “in about the year 1750” and expelled the Dakota (a battle there is recorded in 1745)
source: Wikipedia, “Battle of Kathio” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: 1745: Ortiz places the Kitsai on the upper Trinity, Brazos and Red rivers (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 568

source_says: After abandoning Mille Lacs in the mid-18th century the Mdewakanton settle on the Rum River, and a few years later move their villages to the Mississippi and lower Minnesota (date ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 727

source_says: 1748–49: French deserters pass two Wichita villages a mile and a half apart on the west side of the Arkansas (Deer Creek and Bryson-Paddock), population 1,500–2,500, mostly Taovaya (a partial count)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, p. 550

source_says: “by 1750 their population seems to have exceeded ten thousand and was probably approaching fifteen thousand”; “numbering between ten and fifteen thousand at midcentury”
source: Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008), pp. 66, 102

source_says: Fort de Cavagnial (1744–64), on the bluffs above Salt Creek north of Fort Leavenworth, “roughly in the same location as a major Kansa village”
source: Wikipedia, “Fort de Cavagnial” (site coordinates and participants); Wikipedia, “Kaw people” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Clark, 20 Oct. 1804: old fortified Mandan villages below the Heart River; the Arikara chief “tels me that nation lived in a number villages on each side of the river and the Troubleson Seauex caused them to move about 40 miles higher up”
source: Lewis & Clark journals, ed. Moulton (UNL online edition), entries for 19–20 Oct. 1804

source_says: “The Mandan population in 1750 seems to have been about 9,000”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wood and Irwin, “Mandan”, p. 351

source_says: Utz site: “occupied by the Missouri tribe from c. 15th to the late 18th centuries… probably their principal village area during their first contact with Europeans”
source: Wikipedia, “Utz Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Deer Creek and Bryson-Paddock: “18th century fortified villages of the Wichita… along the Arkansas River in Kay County”
source: Wikipedia, “Deer Creek/Bryson Paddock Sites” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: 1752: Jicarilla trading at Pecos with the Carlana (a trading visit; kept off the track)
source: Ortiz, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 10: Southwest (1983), Tiller, “Jicarilla Apache”, p. 450

source_says: 1752: seeking better trade, the Kansa move their village to the Kansas River near its confluence with the Missouri
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, p. 464

source_says: Louisiana governor, 1754: about 950 warriors (Din and Nasatir)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey, “Osage”, p. 492

source_says: Very shoal water. Here we left our Canoes and travelled 4 miles S.W.b.S. Here were our Indians Families in a starving condition, for want of food; and we are in the same condition. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 326 (pdf 26), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 27 July 1754

source_says: Came to two tents of Asinepoet Indians. I smoaked with them, and talked with them to go down with me to York Fort in the summer, but they answered, “We are conveniently supplied from the Pagua-Mistagushewuck Whiskeheginish.” That is, the Frenchman’s House of Trade. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 327 (pdf 27), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 31 July 1754

source_says: Met with 7 tents of Asinepoet Indians. I smoaked with them,—but have no hopes of getting them to the Fort,—as what cloth &c. they had were French, and, by their behaviour, I perceived they were strongly attached to the French interest. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 327 (pdf 27), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 4 Aug. 1754

source_says: Passed several ponds, & one creek of running water, in which we caught 17 small Trout. In the evening came to 24 tents of Asinepoet Indians. They have plenty of moose & Beaver flesh, with which they treated us liberally. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 330 (pdf 30), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 27 Aug. 1754

source_says: Seven tents of Indians pitched another way. We are yet above 400 in number, two-thirds of whom live chiefly on fruit. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 331 (pdf 31), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 1 Sept. 1754

source_says: We are yet in Muscuty plains. Here are a great many Asinepoet Indians. The Buffalo has taken the route upwards, and is the reason we have not yet met with Archithinue Natives (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 331 (pdf 31), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 5 Sept. 1754

source_says: met with five tents of Mekesue, or Eagle Indians. ... I could perceive no difference between them and the Asinepoet Natives with regard to the language ... The Natives inform me that they are a tribe of that brave Nation; and take their name from Eagles being plenty in the district they inhabit. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 331 (pdf 31), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 6 Sept. 1754

source_says: Henday meets “Asinepoets” (“thought by some to be Assiniboines”) on 20 Sept. 1754, nine days after crossing into present Alberta near Chauvin
source: Wikipedia, “Anthony Henday” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: No Musketoes to trouble us; Travelled 7 Miles W.S.W. Level lands, & small hommocks of woods. Joined by more Asinepoet Indians, who have 6 pack-horses loaded with provisions, &c. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 335 (pdf 35), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 30 Sept. 1754

source_says: Came to us 7 tents of Archithinue Indians; the men all mounted on Horse-back, with Bows and Arrows, & bone spears & darts. I gave the Leader a foot of tobacco, one fire Steel, a string of beads, a knife; and smoked with them. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 335 (pdf 35), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 1 Oct. 1754

source_says: 14–17 Oct. 1754 (Archithinue, Cocking’s general term for the Gros Ventre and the three Blackfoot tribes; “Wissler … was reasonably certain that they also were Gros Ventres”: Ewers, The Horse in Blackfoot Indian Culture (BAE Bulletin 159, 1955), pp. 17–18; Morton: “here the Bloods, for Henday was in their country, which was south of the upper waters of the Red Deer River”, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 247; the people disputed, so kept off the division tracks): Henday “came to 200 tents of Archithinue Natives, pitched in two rows”; on the 17th “322 tents of Archithinue Natives unpitched and moved Westward”. Burpee places the camp southwest of the Red Deer crossing near Knee Hills Creek; others put it west of Pine Lake near Innisfail. Which people is disputed: Burpee reads Blackfoot, Ewers probably Gros Ventre; placed with the Siksika, the northernmost Blackfoot
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), pp. 337–40 (pdf 37–40)

source_says: 322 tents of Archithinue Natives unpitched and moved Westward; 17 tents of Asinepoet Natives moved Northwards; and we moved S.W.b.W. 9 Miles. (place ours) (part; Henday’s Alberta “Assiniboine” were “doubtless Stoneys”: Handbook 13, p. 596)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 340 (pdf 40), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 17 Oct. 1754

source_says: “The earliest known contact of Gros Ventre with whites was around 1754, between the north and south forks of the Saskatchewan River”
source: Wikipedia, “Gros Ventre” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Clear frosty weather. Travelled 6 Miles S.E. Plains & Ledges of tall Birch trees. Thaws very little to-day. (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 342 (pdf 42), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 21 Nov. 1754

source_says: Winter 1754–55: Henday, wintering in central Alberta, “acknowledged the assistance of ‘Assiniboine’ families who were doubtless Stoneys” (place ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Getty and Gooding, “Stoney”, p. 596

source_says: An “old” Iowa village on the site of Council Bluffs, seen by Lewis and Clark; occupied within reach of Fort de Cavagnial (1744); date ours, before the move east about 1765
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 434

source_says: “Situated east of the Crows, the Kiowa took possession of the Black Hills… They continued to occupy the Black Hills until about the close of the last century”; the Apache part of their camp circle
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), p. 156

source_says: “Situated east of the Crows, the Kiowa took possession of the Black Hills… They continued to occupy the Black Hills until about the close of the last century”; the Apache part of their camp circle
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), p. 156

source_says: Travelled 6 Miles W.b.S. The Buffalo & Waskesew being gone that way: killed one Buffalo & four Beaver: Level land, plenty of Creeks, & Beaver houses. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 345 (pdf 45), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 12 Jan. 1755

source_says: We were joined by different tribes of Natives, who yearly visited our Settlements: they brought with them several Archithinue Women & Children Captives, with many Scalps quite green: We are now at Archithinue lake, about one mile broad, & a good days journey in length (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 347 (pdf 47), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 27 Feb. 1755

source_says: Henday, with his Cree guide Attickasish and Cree companions, reaches the North Saskatchewan near the mouth of the Sturgeon River, 3 Mar. 1755, and camps while canoes are built; “more fur-laden Indians arrived”; leaves 27 Apr.
source: Wikipedia, “Anthony Henday” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Ten tents came & pitched alongside of us in order to build Canoes. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 348 (pdf 48), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 18 Mar. 1755

source_says: All hands preparing Wood &c for building Canoes: The Asinepoet Natives are building Canoes below us. (place ours) (part; Henday’s Alberta “Assiniboine” were “doubtless Stoneys”: Handbook 13, p. 596)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 348 (pdf 48), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 25 Mar. 1755

source_says: Embarked on board my Canoe, & paddled down the river 34 Miles, in company with 20 Canoes of Assinipoet Natives (place ours) (part; Henday’s Alberta “Assiniboine” were “doubtless Stoneys”: Handbook 13, p. 596)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 349 (pdf 49), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 28 Apr. 1755

source_says: Paddled 10 miles E.b.N. then came to one hundred tents of Archithinue Natives. Their Leader invited me to his tent, and gave me plenty of Buffalo flesh: our Indians bought a great many Wolves from them, for old axes &c. I could not persuade them to go to the Fort. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 350 (pdf 50), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 12 May 1755

source_says: One hundred and twenty seven tents of Archithinue Natives came to us: I bought 30 Wolves’ skins from them, and the Indians purchased great numbers of Wolves, Beaver & Foxes etc. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 350 (pdf 50), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 15 May 1755

source_says: Paddled 30 Miles N.b.E. when we came to 30 tents of Archithinue Natives: I talked with them as I did with the others; but all to no purpose. Our Indians traded a great many Furs from them. They have the finest Horses I have yet seen here (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 351 (pdf 51), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 16 May 1755; Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 212, n. 52: another version of the journal, B.239/a/40, “specifically mentions meeting ‘bloody Indians’ on 16 May 1755”

source_says: Ten tents of Eagle Indians joined the Archithinue Indians. Five Canoes of them are going to the Fort with me. They are a tribe of the Asinepoet Nation; and like them use the Horses for carrying the baggage and not to ride on. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 351 (pdf 51), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 17 May 1755

source_says: Seventy tents of Archithinue Natives came to us, headed by the Leader that I saw in the Muscuty Country ... They had very few Wolves or Furs of any kind, having traded them before with the Pegogamaw Indians who are gone to the Fort. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 351 (pdf 51), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 21 May 1755

source_says: Paddled none: mustered my Gang total 70 Canoes. (place ours) (part)
source: Henday’s journal, 1754–55, in Burpee, ed., “York Factory to the Blackfeet Country” (1907), p. 353 (pdf 53), Henday (Burpee ed. 1907), entry of 3 June 1755

source_says: By 1757 the Taovaya have moved to the Red River just west of the Western Cross Timbers: a fortified village on the north bank (Longest site), an Iscani village downstream
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, p. 550

source_says: Lipan gather at Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá, 1757
source: Wikipedia, “Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Kerlerec: 150 Missouria men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Kerlerec

source_says: Kerlerec: 800 men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Liberty, Wood, and Irwin, “Omaha”, p. 415, table 2, citing Kerlerec

source_says: Kerlerec: 100 Otoe men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Kerlerec

source_says: Kerlerec: the Panimaha, on the Platte 25 leagues from its mouth, number 600 men bearing arms
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, pp. 518, 563

source_says: Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá near present Menard attacked by “a force of some 2,000 Comanches and allied tribes”, March 1758 (a war expedition, kept off the division track)
source: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online, “Comanche Indians”

source_says: March 1758: Tonkawas join the Comanche, Taovaya and others in sacking the San Sabá mission (a raid; kept off the track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb and Campbell, “Tonkawa”, p. 955

source_says: Parrilla’s attack on the Taovaya twin villages on the Red River, Oct. 1759
source: Wikipedia, “Battle of the Twin Villages” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: At separation from the Sioux (traditional date c. 1760) “at least 1,500 lodges, averaging six souls to a lodge”; then about the head of the Minnesota & Des Moines, Devils Lake, Lac qui Parle
source: Denig, “Indian Tribes of the Upper Missouri” (BAE 46th Annual Report, 1930), p. 396; Hodge’s editor notes the date is far too late

source_says: Big Hidatsa village, “occupied between ca. 1740 and 1850”, Knife River
source: Wikipedia, “Big Hidatsa Village Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: An estimate of 1760: 1,100 souls
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: “About 1760 they moved east and came to live along the Mississippi between the Iowa and Des Moines Rivers”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Mid-18th century: Yanktonai territory from Big Stone Lake and Lake Traverse west to the Missouri (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: Mid-18th century: Yanktonai territory from Big Stone Lake and Lake Traverse west to the Missouri (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: Mid-18th century: Yankton territory the lower Big Sioux and the heads of the Floyd, Little Sioux and Des Moines (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: 1762: the two leaders at the El Cañón missions had 700 followers, and ten other local groups were known: “between 3,000 and 4,000 Lipans living in central Texas” (Tunnell and Newcomb)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Opler, “Lipan Apache”, p. 942

source_says: Lipan at the El Cañón missions on the upper Nueces, 1762–71
source: Mission San Lorenzo de la Santa Cruz (El Cañón) (recalled; not checked against the text this round)

source_says: Biesterfeldt site, occupied c. 1724–1780
source: Wikipedia, “Biesterfeldt Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: From the 1760s to 1851 the Mdewakanton villages stand on the Mississippi and the lower Minnesota (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, pp. 727–29

source_says: 1760s: the Wahpekute villages on the Cannon River and at Traverse des Sioux (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 729

source_says: 1760s: the Wahpeton villages on the Minnesota, above the Mdewakanton (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 727

source_says: William Pink reports a small group of Assiniboines in the Prince Albert area with many horses; they had given up canoes (a single group; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie and Miller, “Assiniboine”, p. 574

source_says: 1765 and the years following: the Iowa move east near the mouth of the Des Moines (On the Des Moines River, 1765–1837)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 435

source_says: Spring 1767: building canoes on the North Saskatchewan above Mooswa Creek, Pink “was visited by a large band of Archithinues, probably Blackfeet” (a visit to the river, kept off the division track)
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 278

source_says: May 1767: two days below, Pink “came on Archithinues of a different kind, and at war with his earlier visitors. These would be the Gros Ventres or Fall Indians” (on the river to trade; kept off the division track)
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 278

source_says: 1768: Fray Gaspar José de Solís visits encampments of Coco, Mayeye, Tonkawa, Yojuane and others on the Brazos northwest of modern College Station
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb and Campbell, “Tonkawa”, pp. 953–54

source_says: Winter 1769–70: Pink and his Assiniboins pass along the north shore of Manitou Lake and winter on the plains beyond, where he “had to do with Blackfeet, Bloods, and Assiniboins”
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 280

source_says: Winter 1769–70: Pink, wintering on the plains beyond Manitou Lake, “had to do with Blackfeet, Bloods, and Assiniboins” (dealings, not their camps; kept off the division tracks)
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 280

source_says: Winter 1769–70: Pink, wintering on the plains beyond Manitou Lake, “had to do with Blackfeet, Bloods, and Assiniboins” (dealings, not their camps; kept off the division tracks)
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), p. 280

source_says: it has come to pass that in despair the Tuacanas, Yscanis, Tancaoueys, and Quitseys have retreated toward the south until they are now in the neighborhood of the presidios of San Saba, Bexar, and Espiritu Santo (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, pp. 167-168 (pdf 174-175), Doc. 30

source_says: “In 1770 when French traders opened relations with them they were a little below Cheyenne River”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Truteau’s pre-epidemic 4,000 warriors (Parks: about 16,000, at least 10,000): 16,000
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Arikara”, p. 387, table 3, citing Truteau’s pre-epidemic 4,000 warriors (Parks: about 16,000, at least 10,000)

source_says: the Taoua'iches nation has been joined recently by another numerous tribe from the Missuris, namely, the Panis-maha, and that these two, having joined the Tuacanas, Caranamez, and Maheys, have gone at the instigation of the Comanchez (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, p. 202 (pdf 209), Doc. 66

source_says: the Tuacanas and Yscanis, immediately upon learning of the wish of the great Captain of La Luiziana, have abandoned the establishment which they had in the vicinity of San Antonio de Vexar and San Saba and are to-day living off to one side, not far from San Pedro (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, p. 212 (pdf 219); cf. p. 214 (pdf 221), Doc. 69

source_says: the Tavai'ases, who, although they form with the foregoing a single nation, live apart for greater convenience in hunting ... have gone to the interior, far to the north, seeking asylum in the dark solitudes which lie between the Natchitoches and Akensas Rivers (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, p. 215 (pdf 222), Doc. 69

source_says: 1772: “something more than 150 warriors, which included Mayeyes and Yojuanes” (Bolton 1914)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb and Campbell, “Tonkawa”, p. 956

source_says: Tawakoni: 36 houses and 120 warriors in the Trinity village, 30 families in the Brazos village (Mézières)
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 303

source_says: Having found the Iscanis scattered about and settled on different farms, I encouraged them to unite to form a single village ... They comprise sixty warriors, and many more women and children. ... They live at a distance of eight leagues westward from the Quitseys pueblo. (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, pp. 286, 289 (pdf 293, 296), Doc. 90

source_says: 1772: De Mézières’ first stop, the Kitsai village on the east side of the Trinity near present Palestine, Texas
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 568

source_says: 1772: the Trinity village “comprised 30 lodges and 80 warriors” (De Mézières)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 568

source_says: The Comanche nation is very large, as is evident to me from the fact that while more than five hundred visited me, the chief men apologized for not having come in greater numbers ... They are divided into various tribes or bands, named Naitanes, Yarambicas, etc. (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, p. 297 (pdf 304), Doc. 90

source_says: The other, called the village of the Taouaiaz, is sixty leagues farther up towards the northeast, on the banks of the Natchitoches River, at the foot of a ridge which furnishes this river its chief supply of water. (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, p. 294 (pdf 301), Doc. 90

source_says: De Mézières’s 1772 report: the Wichita and Taovaya together 600 warriors; the Tawakoni of the Trinity village 120 (36 houses); the Iscani 60, scattered on farms; with a second Tawakoni village on the Brazos of 30 families (not counted here) (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, pp. 286–94 (pdf 293–301), Doc. 90

source_says: The Osage nation, established on the Missuris River, and divided into two villages, reaches the number of one thousand men. They are not more than seven regular days' journey from Los Ylinuezes (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, p. 304 (pdf 311), Doc. 90

source_says: a spring called Las Puentecitas, in whose neighborhood the nation of the Maheyes, Yocuanas, and Tancagues is usually camped (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 1, p. 308 (pdf 315), Doc. 90 (itinerary appended)

source_says: Cocking travels inland with Pegogamaw Cree, “who met their families at the well-known rendezvous at present James Smith First Nation”, summer 1772 (the Pegogamaw a band of the Saskatchewan Cree, filed with the Fort des Prairies division; a band, kept off the division track)
source: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan, “Cocking, Matthew (1743–99)”; DCB, “Cocking, Matthew”

source_says: We did not proceed. I am informed that there are 18 tents of Natives a short distance off (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 102 (pdf 16), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 12 Aug. 1772

source_says: Travelled 9 miles S.W.b.S., came to a branch of Saskatchewan River, where we put up. ... Here we met with a Leader named Commeseskew, with 14 tents full of natives; They heard of Buffalo up this branch. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 103 (pdf 17), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 22 Aug. 1772

source_says: We did not proceed: Hunters killed several Buffalo. This day I took an Observation per noon Altitude. Latitude 52° 37’ North. (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 104 (pdf 18), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 26 Aug. 1772

source_says: We proceeded all in Company: Our Course West, distance 13 miles. Leaving the river on one hand, came to some high land named Mikisew Wache, or Eagle hills, where we pitched (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 105 (pdf 19), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 6 Sept. 1772

source_says: Ten tents of Asinepoet Natives came to us: they say they left several tents of Asinepoet Natives & Archithinue Natives (their friends) two days’ journey beyond Manitow-Sakahegan. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 106 (pdf 20), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 18 Sept. 1772

source_says: they say they left several tents of Asinepoet Natives & Archithinue Natives (their friends) two days’ journey beyond Manitow-Sakahegan. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 106 (pdf 20), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 18 Sept. 1772

source_says: they say they left several tents of Asinepoet Natives & Archithinue Natives (their friends) two days’ journey beyond Manitow-Sakahegan. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 106 (pdf 20), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 18 Sept. 1772

source_says: Travelled 3 miles S.E.: the Asinepoet Natives that last arrived going N.W.: Others with Neheathaway Indians going easterly: all to trap Wolves, & pound Buffalo; at present only eight tents. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 107 (pdf 21), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 24 Sept. 1772

source_says: We proceeded: Our Course West & distance 2 miles, arriving at the ridge of small poplars where the Natives intend to trap the winter season. Two tents separated from us, going more northerly (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 108 (pdf 22), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 10 Oct. 1772

source_says: Every person repairing the Beast pound. ... This pound was made by our Archithinue friends last spring, who had great success, many Skulls & Bones lying in the pound. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 109 (pdf 23), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 23 Oct. 1772

source_says: From the rendezvous the Pegogamaw make a circuit west to the Eagle Hills and the Thickwood Hills, “hunting out on the open plains southwest of modern Biggar”, autumn–winter 1772–73
source: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan, “Cocking, Matthew (1743–99)”; DCB, “Cocking, Matthew”

source_says: Early December 1772: Cocking meets 28 tepees of Gros Ventre at a buffalo pound near the Eagle Hills; they have already split into winter bands (a band; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Fowler and Flannery, “Gros Ventre”, p. 678

source_says: We were joined by ten tents of Asinepoet Indians. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 112 (pdf 26), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 21 Dec. 1772

source_says: Joined by five tents of Nehetheway Indians. There are but few furs amongst us as yet. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 112 (pdf 26), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 22 Dec. 1772

source_says: Two Asinepoet Natives joined us, they left their people 7 tents, this morning: They say Buffalo are very scarce; plenty of Waskesew but no Ammunition (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 114 (pdf 28), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 3 Feb. 1773

source_says: We proceeded: Our Course N.N.E. & distance 10 miles, where we joined the Asinepoet Natives; & likewise the Natives who left us Yesterday: At present 20 tents of Indians (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 114 (pdf 28), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 5 Feb. 1773

source_says: my Leader with eleven tents of Asinepoet Natives unpitched intending to proceed there: but I with nine tents part; Asinepoet Natives lay still: they intend to build Canoes at Saketow-Wachee. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 115 (pdf 29), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 23 Feb. 1773

source_says: We arrived at the Beast pound, where we met with my Leader again, with 4 tents of Neheathaway & 20 tents of Asinepoet Natives; The last are most part of them unacquainted with Canoes (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 116 (pdf 30), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 27 Mar. 1773

source_says: with 4 tents of Neheathaway & 20 tents of Asinepoet Natives; ... the others, 30 tents of Neheathaway Natives, had unpitched, intending to proceed slowly towards the place of building Canoes, hunting as they go. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 116 (pdf 30), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 27 Mar. 1773

source_says: All hands employed collecting materials & building Canoes. No Snow on the ground, but what is in the Woods. Indian Visitors coming & going; whose people generally employed as we are, preparing Canoes. (place ours) (part)
source: Cocking’s journal, 1772–73, in Burpee, ed., “An Adventurer from Hudson Bay” (1908), p. 117 (pdf 31), Cocking (Burpee ed. 1908), entry of 10 Apr. 1773

source_says: The circuit ends at a bison pound near Red Deer Hill, south of Prince Albert, spring 1773
source: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan, “Cocking, Matthew (1743–99)”; DCB, “Cocking, Matthew”

source_says: On the sixteenth we arrived at the village of the Panis. They are situated in a prairie on the bank of the Red River, west of the Cados one hundred leagues. The name of the nation is Panis. It contains four villages, namely, the Tavoyache, the Ouatchita, the Niscaniche, and the Toyacane. There are in all one thousand warriors. (place ours) (Taovaya, Wichita proper, Iscani and a Tawakoni village together)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 85 (pdf 91), Doc. 136

source_says: 3 July 1774: “The Naytane chief… came with the whole nation”, four bands assembled at the Taovaya village, one of them the Yamparika; Gaignard was told they “comprise fully four thousand warriors” (Hämäläinen dates it 1773 and derives about 16,000; the figure is for the four eastern bands, here applied to the whole nation)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, pp. 93–94 (pdf 99–100), Gaignard’s journal; Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008), p. 102

source_says: it will be necessary for this purpose even to have in the village of the Toicanne and the Anamas, who have united, a trader ... the convoy which was going to the Toicanne a hundred leagues distant from the Panis (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 97 (pdf 103), Doc. 136

source_says: The rumor is spreading among the Indians that the Osages have abandoned their ancient village in order to form another far distant from the first, and far up the Rio de los Arkansas. (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 110 (pdf 116), Doc. 145

source_says: “In the 1770s the Gros Ventres occupied the region near the forks of the Saskatchewan River” (Binnema’s reconstruction)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 75

source_says: “Around 1775 the Omaha developed a new village, probably located near present-day Homer, Nebraska” (Big Village)
source: Wikipedia, “Omaha people” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Winter 1774–75: Peter Pond travels nine days up the Minnesota to a camp of Sioux he calls Yankton (“probably Yanktonai”), some 200 miles above his post (a camp; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: c. 1775 (Hyde’s date): the Oglala cross the Missouri “at the Sioux Pass, just below the Great Bend in the Crow Creek neighborhood” and start up Bad River (the Oglala part of the Teton)
source: Hyde, Red Cloud’s Folk: A History of the Oglala Sioux Indians (1937), pp. 19–20

source_says: Winter 1775–76: Alexander Henry the elder visits the Assiniboins “encamped in a similar island of trees upon the plains somewhere south of Melfort. There might be a hundred tents or more”, later joined by another camp of like size
source: Morton, A History of the Canadian West to 1870–71 (1939), pp. 314–15

source_says: Cruzat, 1777: 250 warriors
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Houck: 200 Missouria warriors
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Houck

source_says: Houck: 100 Otoe warriors
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Houck

source_says: Cruzat, Nov. 1777: the Chawi on the west bank of Skull Creek below the Platte (Barcal site)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: Cruzat, 1777: the Kitkahahki in a village on the Republican River
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: 1777: about 300 Panimahas leave the Skiri on the Loup for the Red River, joining the Taovaya; they stay into the 19th century (part; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: The village of the Osages, which, according to men of experience, contains eight hundred men, is situated on an eminence in the midst of a large plain, in which they pasture their horses and raise their crops (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 144 (pdf 150), Doc. 164

source_says: these Lipanes, Natages, and Mescaleros, are known as Apaches de Oriente [Eastern Apaches] ; that the first live on both sides of the Rio Grande del Norte, under shelter of the presidios of San Juan Bautista, Monclova, and Santa Rosa de Aguaverde, part of them withdrawing at times to the Parage de la Nogalera (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 153 (pdf 159), Doc. 165

source_says: Lehmer: villages reduced between 1750 and 1780, population about 4,400 before the epidemic
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wood and Irwin, “Mandan”, p. 351

source_says: “In 1778, the Taovaya village at Spanish Fort had 123 houses and across the Red River a Wichita town had another 37 houses”
source: Wikipedia, “Taovaya” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Tawehash (Taovaya): two villages of 160 lodges, “800 fighting men and youths”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 303

source_says: And the Comanche nation, whose name is applied generically to various groups of Indians . . . 5000 Total . 7280 (a compiled estimate of warriors)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 166 (pdf 172), Doc. 165

source_says: Council of war at San Antonio, 5 Jan. 1778 (Merino y Moreno, secretary): the Kitsai 90 warriors (a compiled estimate)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, pp. 165–66 (pdf 171–72); DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 570

source_says: Council of war at San Antonio, 5 Jan. 1778 (Merino y Moreno, secretary): the Taovaya 500 warriors, the Tawakoni 250, the Iscani 50 (the Panis-mahas’ 600 not counted here) (a compiled official estimate)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, pp. 165-166 (pdf 171-172), Doc. 165

source_says: the first division may go towards the junction of Rio Puerco with the Rio Grande, the asylum most frequented by the Lipan (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 183 (pdf 189), Doc. 167

source_says: I arrived at the place which the natives call La Tortuga ... The Tancagues live in its neighborhood, not in permanent houses and in a village, but underneath [tents of] skins, and in various bands ... They number about three hundred warriors, including not a few apostates. (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 192 (pdf 198), Doc. 170

source_says: Marching sixteen leagues in the same direction, west, from El Parage de la Tortuga ... I arrived at the bank of the River Brazos de Dios ... the Tuacanas, who have settled on the opposite bank ... This village contains about one hundred fifty warriors. (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, pp. 193, 195 (pdf 199, 201), Doc. 171

source_says: They complain bitterly of the continued thieving of the Comanches, who have settled in large numbers on the same river, the Brazos (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 195 (pdf 201); cf. p. 212 (pdf 218): 'eight of the Comanches who live above the Tuacanas on the bank of the Brazos River', Docs. 171 & 181

source_says: Continuing in the same westward direction, at a distance of eight leagues above the former village I found another settlement of the Tuacanas on the bank of the same Brazos River ... The character of the people, who exceed the former in number, is the same (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, pp. 196-197 (pdf 202-203), Doc. 172

source_says: 18 Apr. 1778, De Mézières at the Spanish Fort villages: “The nation of the Taovayazes is divided into two villages”, 37 houses on the north bank of the Red River and 123 on the opposite bank, 10–12 beds to a house, “more than eight hundred” men and youths (the Handbook dates the visit 1779 and calls the north-bank town Wichita proper; De Mézières calls both Taovaya)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, pp. 201–2 (pdf 207–8), De Mézières to Croix, 18 Apr. 1778; DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, p. 551

source_says: The nation of the Taovayazes is divided into two villages, one situated on the northern bank of the Vermejo, or Natchitoches, River, the other opposite the first on the other bank. The former is composed of thirty-seven houses, the latter of one hundred twenty-three. ... more than eight hundred (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, pp. 201-202 (pdf 207-208), Doc. 175

source_says: 1778: a small Kitsai village of 20 warriors, separated from the larger one, near present Grand Saline, Texas (part of the people)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 568

source_says: Tawakoni: the two towns, then on the Brazos, held “more than 300 warriors” (Mézières, 1778–79)
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 303

source_says: Voget: “a population between 8,000 and 10,000 before the smallpox epidemics of 1781”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Voget, “Crow”, p. 714

source_says: Clark, 22 Oct. 1804: “the upper of the 6 Villages the Mandans occupied about 25 years ago… entirely cut off by the Sioux”
source: Lewis & Clark journals, ed. Moulton (UNL online edition), entry for 22 Oct. 1804

source_says: Being now in the village of the Quitseis, I am going to continue for the Tuacanas by the same route as last year. (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 265 (pdf 271), Doc. 217

source_says: Anza defeats Cuerno Verde, “probably a Jupe war chief” (Hämäläinen), near the Greenhorn Mountains, 3 Sept. 1779, after surprising his ranchería of 120 lodges; Kavanagh: the battles of 1774 and 1779 were in the area Miera’s map gives the Jupes
source: Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008), pp. 103, 110; Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), p. 93; Wikipedia, “Cuerno Verde” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Two leagues from the first village of the Tuacanas I met a large party of the Tancagues, who were awaiting me there. They at once dispatched messengers and made signals with smoke, in order to report my arrival to others, who were hunting in the vicinity. (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 269 (pdf 275), Doc. 222

source_says: The Tancagues remain since the last epidemic at the number of one hundred fifty; the Tuacanas, to whom it was very fatal, have one hundred men more; among the Indians of San Theodoro and the Panis-mahas, where it fell with less force, there was not so great a diminution; among the Comanches, none. (place ours)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 274 (pdf 280); Croix's summary vol. 2, p. 313 (pdf 319), Doc. 223

source_says: The Tancagues remain since the last epidemic at the number of one hundred fifty; the Tuacanas, to whom it was very fatal, have one hundred men more (place ours) (part)

source_says: the Lipanes, who were staying in this vicinity, watching them and intending to attack them on their way out (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 322 (pdf 328), Doc. 238

source_says: set out for the Colorado River to accompany the Tancagues, who were returning to their lands (which precaution was taken by the chevalier governor, in view of the threats made by the Lipanes, who were staying in this vicinity, watching them (place ours) (part)
source: Bolton, ed., Athanase de Mézières and the Louisiana–Texas Frontier, 1768–1780 (1914), vol. 2, p. 322 (pdf 328), Doc. 238

source_says: Nov. 1779: the first recorded Gros Ventre visit to Hudson House (a trading visit)

source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 386

source_says: About 3,000 Arikara in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 274

source_says: 10,000 Assiniboin in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 388

source_says: Cheyenne and Sutaio 3,500 in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: 4,000 Crow in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Estimates of Comanche numbers in 1780, when most numerous, “are usually around 20,000”

source_says: 3,000 Atsina in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Hidatsa and Amahami together 2,500 in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: 3,000 Kansa in 1780

source_says: “About 25 years since they lived in six villages, about forty miles below their present villages”

source_says: About 2,800 Omaha in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 286

source_says: 6,200 Osage in 1780

source_says: About 900 Oto in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: 800 Ponca in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: 10,000 Pawnee in 1780

source_says: Mooney: 15,000 in 1780

source_says: “25,000 Dakota of all divisions, exclusive of the Assiniboin” in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 283

source_says: The confederated Wichita tribes about 3,200 in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: The Mandan villages around the mouth of the Heart River abandoned about 1780; the survivors move up near the mouth of the Knife (Lewis and Clark)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, p. 255

source_says: Crow tradition told to Bradley (1876): “the greater portion making their home upon the waters of the Powder River, while the smaller band of four hundred lodges, or about four thousand souls, were camped in the lower extremity of the Clark’s Fork bottom”, where the smallpox struck (one band; date about 1781)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 127 (Bradley, “Journal”, p. 166)

source_says: Hämäläinen’s high reckoning: a 1785 account gives the eastern Comanches 2,000 fighting men after losing two-thirds to smallpox, so “the total Comanche population in the early 1780s reached or exceeded forty thousand”
source: Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008), pp. 102–3

source_says: Tradition: 800 lodges before the smallpox (Denig: 1776–77; Ewers, n. 21: 1781–82), about 400 after, “about 1,200 persons” dead
source: Denig, Five Indian Tribes of the Upper Missouri, ed. Ewers (1961), pp. 109, 114–15

source_says: Survivors of the 1781 smallpox, about 2,000
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Stewart, “Hidatsa”, p. 329

source_says: The 1781 smallpox epidemic “left only 1,000–1,500 individuals”

source_says: Miró: seven Arikara villages on the Missouri below the Cheyenne River

source_says: Mid-1780s: “according to Spanish observers, the western Comanches alone numbered between sixteen and eighteen thousand, while a 1785 account states that the eastern Comanches had two thousand fighting men, which translates into a total eastern Comanche population of some eight thousand”

source_says: Miró, 1785: the “Pados” in “small forts” near the Bad River, in four small wandering groups (the first unambiguous reference to the Plains Apache)

source_says: Miró, 1785: the Pados “number about three hundred and fifty men”

source_says: “As early as the 1780s, Ojibwas were observed at trading posts along the Assiniboine River catering to a largely Plains clientele” (a range; centre ours)

source_says: Miró, 1785: the Ponca “probably” on Bazile Creek, just below the mouth of the Niobrara
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Brown and Irwin, “Ponca”, p. 416

source_says: Miró, 1785: 400 “men capable of bearing arms”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 563

source_says: Miró, 1785: 220 “men capable of bearing arms”

source_says: Miró, 1785: 350 “men capable of bearing arms”

source_says: Vial and Chaves reach the twin Taovaya villages near Spanish Fort, 6 Aug. 1785
