source: Wikipedia, “Comanche–Spanish peace treaties”

source_says: Pecos, 28 Feb.–3 Mar. 1786: “two hundred Comanche chiefs waited in Pecos” for the treaty and trade fair with Anza (a delegation, kept off the division track)
source: Wikipedia, “Comanche–Spanish peace treaties”

source_says: Spring 1786: eight Kotsoteka rancherías of 700 lodges in an area 40 leagues square; “at 12 residents each, there were 8,400 persons”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Kavanagh, “Comanche”, p. 900

source_says: Anza, 1786: “the Jupes and Yamparicas extending from the Rio Napestle [Arkansas] to the north a little beyond the Sierra de Almagre. Many others … are farther along in the same direction”
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), p. 123

source_says: Anza, 1786: five Jupe local bands, “with a total of 223 lodges, all north of the Arkansas River” (the Jupe then outnumbered the Yamparika, whose lieutenant general was a Jupe)
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), pp. 124–25

source_says: Anza, 1786: “the Jupes and Yamparicas extending from the Rio Napestle [Arkansas] to the north a little beyond the Sierra de Almagre. Many others … are farther along in the same direction”
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), p. 123

source_says: Anza, 1786: perhaps six Yamparika local bands with a total of 108 lodges north of the Arkansas; “many others … are farther along in the same direction” (a partial count)
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), pp. 123–25

source_says: Vial winters “among the Comanche near Wichita Falls”, 1786–87 (the eastern Comanche: Kavanagh, p. 97)
source: Wikipedia, “Pedro Vial” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: July 1787: at Paruanarimuca’s request Anza sends a master builder and thirty laborers to build adobe houses and corrals for the Jupes “on the upper Arkansas River near the Rocky Mountains” (San Carlos de los Jupes, near present Pueblo; site after Thomas 1929)
source: Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008), pp. 126–27

source_says: Thompson winters with the Piegan: “Arrive at the Bow River. Cross it. Meet Peeagans… Lodge with an old man” (Saukamappee), winter 1787–88
source: David Thompson’s Narrative of His Explorations in Western America, 1784–1812, ed. Tyrrell (Champlain Society, 1916), p. 54 and ch. XXIII (pp. 345 ff.)

source_says: 1 July 1788, three leagues east of modern Tucumcari: Vial’s party meets “a rancheria of fifty-six lodges under Naisaras”
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), p. 139

source_says: July 1788: a Comanche village of 372 lodges on the upper Red River (Loomis and Nasatir; western Kotsoteka or eastern Comanche, not known)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Kavanagh, “Comanche”, p. 900

source_says: “Next to them, and who extend to the confluence of the South and North Branch, are the Fall or Big-bellied Indians… about six hundred warriors”
source: Mackenzie (1801), quoted in Hayden, Contributions to the Ethnography and Philology of the Indian Tribes of the Missouri Valley (1862), p. 253

source_says: “Next to them, on the same water, are the Blood Indians… fifty tents, or two hundred and fifty men”
source: Mackenzie (1801), quoted in Hayden, Contributions to the Ethnography and Philology of the Indian Tribes of the Missouri Valley (1862), p. 253

source_says: “On the head waters of the South Branch [Saskatchewan] are the Picaneux, to the number of twelve to fifteen hundred men”
source: Mackenzie, General History of the Fur Trade (1801), quoted in Hayden, Contributions to the Ethnography and Philology of the Indian Tribes of the Missouri Valley (1862), p. 253

source_says: Munier licensed “to trade with the Ponca at the mouth of the Niobrara River”, 1789
source: Wikipedia, “Ponca” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: “From them downwards extend the Blackfeet Indians… their number may be eight hundred men”
source: Mackenzie (1801), quoted in Hayden, Contributions to the Ethnography and Philology of the Indian Tribes of the Missouri Valley (1862), p. 253

source_says: Aug. 1789: near Palo Duro Canyon the New Mexicans meet the ranchería of Ecueracapa, the Kotsoteka principal chief
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), p. 139

source_says: Clark’s map shows “some six old villages in present Oliver County, below Hensler, some of them indicated as having been abandoned nine years, that is, since 1795” (Moulton)
source: Lewis & Clark journals, ed. Moulton (UNL online edition), with Moulton’s notes, 24 Oct. 1804, n. 3

source_says: “Here, or in the immediate neighborhood, they remained until 1798, when they suffered a terrible defeat at the hands of the Sauk and Fox”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Nanza (Ponca Fort): “a fortified village built by the Ponca… circa 1700 and occupied until about 1865”
source: Wikipedia, “Ponca Fort” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Hill site: “a village of the Kitkehahki band… in a region of the Republican River valley that they occupied intermittently from the 1770s to the 1820s”
source: Wikipedia, “Pike-Pawnee Village Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Umfreville, 1790: “a small tribe which has separated from the main body, and now harbor in some country about the Stony [Rocky] Mountains” (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Dempsey, “Sarcee”, p. 629

source_says: Pedro Vial taken by the Kaw to “their village on the Kansas River”, 1792
source: Wikipedia, “Pedro Vial” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Dec. 1792: Shoshone emissaries visit “large Piegan encampments near the Highwood River”; Fidler winters with Sakatow’s band
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 138 (Fidler, E.3/2)

source_says: “Sarcee bands pounded bison as far south as the Battle River by 1793”
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 175

source_says: Nov. 1793: the Kotsoteka meet “along the [Canadian]” to elect a successor to Ecueracapa
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), pp. 143, 190

source_says: Autumn 1794 (Truteau): Brulés with Yankton visitors stop Truteau at the lower end of the Great Bend; one band of 22 lodges hunts west of the Missouri on White River
source: Hyde, Red Cloud’s Folk: A History of the Oglala Sioux Indians (1937), p. 26 (Truteau)

source_says: Winter 1794–95 (M’Gillivray at Fort George): the Strong Wood and Grand River bands build buffalo pounds near the fort; the Canoe band comes in to trade (two bands; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie and Miller, “Assiniboine”, p. 574

source_says: Truteau, 1795: the Arapaho (Caminanbiches) live on the headwaters of the Cheyenne River in western South Dakota and eastern Wyoming, near the Kiowa (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Fowler, “Arapaho”, p. 840

source_says: 1790s (Mackenzie): the western Assiniboine bands in eastern Alberta near Fort George on the North Saskatchewan, some in the woodlands north of the river
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie and Miller, “Assiniboine”, p. 574

source_says: After the Ojibwe destroyed the Sheyenne River town, “a number of villages belonging to the tribe along the Missouri near the point where the boundary line between North and South Dakota crosses it”; Ordway passes “an old village some years ago of the Chien Nation”, 15 Oct. 1804
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952); Lewis & Clark journals, ed. Moulton (UNL online edition), entry for 15 Oct. 1804

source_says: Truteau, 1795: the Kiowa live near the Arapaho on the headwaters of the Cheyenne River (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Fowler, “Arapaho”, p. 840

source_says: “By the 1790s, a steadily growing number were utilizing the prairies west of the Red River as far as the Pembina Hills”; also reported on the Souris, Qu’Appelle and Saskatchewan, but not settled there until the 19th century (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Albers, “Plains Ojibwa”, p. 653

source_says: “About ten years since, they boasted 700 warriors” (village 236 mi above the Platte)
source: Clark/Lewis, printed “Statistical View of the Indian Nations,” 1806 (remarks paragraphs in the UNL edition of the Estimate)

source_says: “About ten years since they withdrew… and established a village on a large northwardly branch of the Kanzas” (Republican R.)
source: Clark/Lewis, printed “Statistical View of the Indian Nations,” 1806 (remarks paragraphs in the UNL edition of the Estimate)

source_says: Jan. 1795, Bird at Nipawin: “the seventy tents of the Saskatchewan, Red Deer…, Swan, and Red River Cree bands” gathering against the Gros Ventre (part; place ours)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), pp. 187–88

source_says: After a short war with the Osage, the Spanish build Fort Carondelet in 1795 near their villages on the Osage River
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Swagerty, “History of the United States Plains Until 1850”, p. 266

source_says: In 1796 the Arikara lived in “two consolidated villages just below the mouth of the Cheyenne River”
source: Historical Marker Database, “Arikara villages” marker (hmdb.org, marker 113316)

source_says: Truteau, 1796: the Pados live on the southwest branch of the Platte (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Foster and McCollough, “Plains Apache”, p. 928

source_says: Truteau: 1,100
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Liberty, Wood, and Irwin, “Omaha”, p. 415, table 2, citing Truteau

source_says: 1796: expecting a Sioux attack, the Arikara abandon their two villages below the Cheyenne; one group goes north to the Mandan, the others west to the Cheyenne (Truteau) (kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Arikara”, p. 366

source_says: 14 Dec. 1796: “four hundred Gros Ventres arrived at Edmonton” to reconcile with the traders (a trading visit; persons or men not stated)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 187 (B.60/a/2)

source_says: Dec. 1797, on the Souris: “five Tents of Stone Indians”, then “eight tents of Stone Indians”
source: David Thompson’s Narrative of His Explorations in Western America, 1784–1812, ed. Tyrrell (Champlain Society, 1916), pp. 212–14

source_says: “The Fall Indians of 128 houses, and seven tents have a population of 1330 souls, of which 190 are warriors” (ten to a house); upper village 31 houses and 7 tents, Great Village 82 houses on the Knife River
source: David Thompson’s Narrative of His Explorations in Western America, 1784–1812, ed. Tyrrell (Champlain Society, 1916), pp. 226–28

source_says: “This will give to the Mandanes for 190 houses, a population of 1520 souls; of which they may muster about 220 warriors” (eight to a house)
source: David Thompson’s Narrative of His Explorations in Western America, 1784–1812, ed. Tyrrell (Champlain Society, 1916), pp. 226–28

source_says: Z. Trudeau: 600 men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Liberty, Wood, and Irwin, “Omaha”, p. 415, table 2, citing Z. Trudeau

source_says: Trudeau, 1798: 400 men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1

source_says: Zenon Trudeau, 1798: 800 men for the “Panis” on the Platte (the South Bands)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 563

source_says: 1 Feb. 1798: “eight Tents of Stone Indians, in the same place as [when] we went”
source: David Thompson’s Narrative of His Explorations in Western America, 1784–1812, ed. Tyrrell (Champlain Society, 1916), p. 240

source_says: “Their principal town was on the Des Moines River and for a long time at a spot in the northwestern part of Van Buren County”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: By 1800 the Sisseton on Big Stone Lake and Lake Traverse, joined by most of the Wahpeton (a range)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, pp. 727–29

source_says: By 1800 most of the Wahpeton have joined the Sisseton at Big Stone Lake and Lake Traverse (a range)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 729

source_says: Tabeau, about 1800: the Arapaho live between the Yellowstone and the Platte (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Fowler, “Arapaho”, p. 840

source_says: About 1800: Arikara traders meet the Arapaho, Kiowa and Plains Apache at a trade fair in the Black Hills (Tabeau)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Fowler, “Arapaho”, p. 840

source_says: Nov. 1800: Thompson and McGillivray visit “Sakatow’s Piegan band at Spitcheyee (near present-day High River, Alberta)” (one band)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 169

source_says: Fidler at Chesterfield House, 1800: “the Gros Ventres consisted of about 180 tents with about 600 warriors”; the post was “situated near the Gros Ventre wintering grounds”
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 189 (Fidler, B.39/a/1; Johnson, Saskatchewan Journals)

source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Dempsey, “Sarcee”, p. 636, table 2

source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, p. 551

source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 152, fig. 7.5 (HBCA E.3/2, fols. 105d–6)

source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 152, fig. 7.5 (HBCA E.3/2, fols. 105d–6)

source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 152, fig. 7.5 (HBCA E.3/2, fols. 105d–6)

source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 152, fig. 7.5 (HBCA E.3/2, fols. 105d–6)

source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 152, fig. 7.5 (HBCA E.3/2, fols. 105d–6)

source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 189

source_says: Late Aug. 1801: twenty-eight more Gros Ventres killed “on the upper Oldman River near present-day Lethbridge” (one camp)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 189

source_says: 2 Oct. 1801: “Fidler estimated that 1,400 Indian men, women, and children were camped at the posts at Chesterfield House”; most were Siksika and Gros Ventre
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 171

source_says: 31 Oct. 1801, Fidler: about twenty “Tatood Indians”, Arapaho escorted by the Gros Ventre, forty-four days from the south; “a pretty numerous tribe amounting to about 90 or 100 tents” (part: one Arapaho group)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 171 (B.39/a/2)

source_says: 1 Mar. 1802: “the entire Gros Ventre band, together with Arapaho guests, was camped at Chesterfield House”
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 191 (B.39/a/2)

source_says: By 15 Apr. 1802: “every Fall Indian with their families are pitched away for the Mis sis su rie River” (Little Bear to Fidler; destination only)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), pp. 191–92 (B.39/a/2)

source_says: 1802: “Charles Le Raye visited the Crows in the upper Yellowstone and lower Bighorn Valleys”
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 182 (Le Raye)

source_says: Aug. and Oct. 1802: Le Raye meets “Paunched Indians”, whom Binnema takes as “certainly Gros Ventre-Arapahos”, in the foothills of the upper Yellowstone; they lived on the upper Yellowstone and the Bighorn (one band)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), p. 192 (Le Raye)

source_says: Henry returns to his Pembina River post, Sept. 1802: “60 Saulteurs camped at my fort”
source: Alexander Henry the younger, journal of the Pembina River post, in Coues ed., New Light… (1897), vol. 1, p. 203

source_says: Le Raye, Oct. 1802: the Shoshone nation “resides principally on the headwaters of the Big Horn river, and in the most inaccessible parts of the Rocky mountains” (the narrative’s authenticity is doubted by some)
source: Binnema, Common and Contested Ground: A Human and Environmental History of the Northwestern Plains (2001), pp. 182–83 (Le Raye)

source_says: Council with the Yankton “at the lower point of Calumet Bluff”, 30 Aug. 1804
source: Lewis & Clark journals, ed. Moulton (UNL online edition), entry for 30 Aug. 1804

source_says: Council with the Teton band of Black Buffalo at the mouth of the Teton (Bad) River, 25 Sept. 1804; the people “came flocking in from both sides of the river”

source_says: Clark’s three Arapaho groups: Kanenavich, 150 lodges, 400 warriors, 1,500 souls (heads of the N. Platte & S. fork of the Cheyenne); Staetan (“Kites”), 25 lodges, 75 warriors, 300 souls (head of the Cheyenne, often with the Kanenavich); Nemousin (“Allebome”), 15 lodges, 50 warriors, 200 souls (head of the N. fork of the Cheyenne). The Staetan are Tabeau’s Squihitanes, of the same language as the Arapaho, and the Nemousin his Nimoussines, the Nawathinehena (Fowler, “Arapaho”, Handbook 13 (2001), pp. 860–61)
source: Clark, “Estimate of the Eastern Indians,” Fort Mandan, winter 1804–05 (Moulton ed., Journals of the Lewis & Clark Expedition, vol. 3; UNL online edition)

source_says: Clark: the Staetan (“Kites”), an Arapaho group, at the head of the Cheyenne, often with the Kanenavich (part; kept off the division track)
source: Clark, “Estimate of the Eastern Indians,” Fort Mandan, winter 1804–05 (Moulton ed., Journals of the Lewis & Clark Expedition, vol. 3; UNL online edition); identification Fowler, “Arapaho”, Handbook 13 (2001), p. 860

source_says: Clark: the Nemousin (“Allebome”), the Nawathinehena division of the Arapaho, at the head of the north fork of the Cheyenne (part; kept off the division track)

source_says: on their way in, they saw on Pecan Bayou at the two Great hills a large number of Comanche coming towards the Villages on this river they were Mopechucope's the Hoish band, he was with them, he said he was going to the Caddo villages Red Bear's house for ear Corn (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 50

source_says: the Comanche were of the Yamparika bands who inhabit high up on the Canadian in New Mexico (place ours)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 50

source_says: whilst traveling on Walnut Bayou we met with some Waco whoom informed us that the Wichita had deserted those Villages and gone with the Comanche to the Clear Fork of the Brazos (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 77

source_says: we then left for the Comanche on the Clear Fork of Brazos after traveling some nine or ten days through the heat on tired animals we found the Comanche about two hundred miles from the Keechi Village after our arrival we held a council with the Comanche whoom all appeared to be well disposed but the young man (Buffalo Hump) (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 74

source_says: on our rout we passed through the Waco and Tawakoni villages which we found all evacuated none of them to be found; though we found plenty of peas and pumpkins ... then they removed to the mouth of the Clear Fork of the Brazos whare we understand they still remain (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 77

source_says: on the 12th of Sept we landed at the Keechi village whare we found James Shaw with the Comanche ... we also found some of the Waco and Tawakoni; on the following day we met the Comanche Keechi Waco Tawakoni and Caddo in Council (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 77

source_says: Comanche Chief “I do not think that my people will go in that direction, there are many bad indians traveling through there, the Kiowa are now at war with your people. I shall stay on this river and in this direction.” ... “The Comanche never understood it so, when the buffalo come below there is nothing for us to eat above.” (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. Nos. 75-76

source_says: I returned to the Tonkawa camp on the Colorado—where I found the women picking out cotton and many of the men lying about Bastrop drunk ... I came by Tonkawa Encamped on the head of Buckners Creek (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 111

source_says: We then proceeded in the direction of the Waco Village and after proceeding some 15 miles came upon the Tawakoni Village ... We then proceeded to the Waco Village where we arrived on the 1st Nov. (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 103

source_says: they all stated to me that the Comanche Kiowa Arapaho and Cheyenne were counseling together in large numbers with Buffalo Hump and his party
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 103

source_says: About 800 Jicarilla in 1845
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 371

source_says: The Buffalo are close by here, and we are obliged to come down with our families among them ... In the Spring some of my men will be down about San Antonio ... We shall rang[e] from the Colorado to the Guadalupe (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 129

source_says: It appears that the information had that the Lipan were on the Bosque was erroneous; Ramon Castro one of their Captains and another individual of are now here, they say their Camp is on the Cibolo—San Baitolo—near the Crossing of the La Bahía Road. (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 169

source_says: I am happy to find that the Tonkawa Indians are all collected together on the hunting grounds designated for their use that they are doing well and are contented and that game is in abundance. (place ours)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 195

source_says: Information has just been recd at this office of the arrival at the trading House on the Brazos of a party of Comanche, and that the main body of them Consisting of about 1000. Lodges are encamped on Little River, they are bound Westward to redress their wrongs beyond the Rio Grande (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. Nos. 204

source_says: I found about 30 Comanche in Their camp on the Borrego [Boregas Creek] ... they say they belong to Santa Anna party.
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 124

source_says: I found that there main camp was on the Borrego [Boregas], a branch of the Atascosa about 50 miles South of San Antonio. A small party of them near Dn. Erasmo Seguins Ranch
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 124

source_says: “List of the chiefs of the Lipan Tribs as they Gave them to me in council”: Lemas Castro, principal chief; Raymond and John Castro, war chiefs; Capt. Roan, Chicito and Chico, civil chiefs; “By thire own account 67. warriers” (Neighbors, report endorsed June 15, 1845; the printed dateline, Jan. 15, is contradicted by the endorsement and the council of 3 June it reports)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 125, table

source_says: with these proceed to the Comanche Village on the waters of Little River and having amicably arranged with Mopechucope. with him proceed to the City of Austin (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 237

source_says: Pah-hah yuco is on the head waters of the Brazos but that he will be down and join Mopechucope. in a short time, as they are in want of meat, and are out of the Buffalo Range where they are. (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 238

source_says: Mopechucope who is now encamped on the Colorado above Austin ... Pah-hah yuco is on the head waters of the Brazos but that he will be down and join Mopechucope. in a short time, as they are in want of meat, and are out of the Buffalo Range where they are. (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 238

source_says: On the 30th Jun I visited the Tonkawa Camp. and found Them Camped on the Cibolo near the old Gonzales crossing.
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 124

source_says: “The River Crows charged a moving Blackfeet camp near Judith Gap in 1845”
source: Wikipedia, “Crow people” (site coordinates and participants) (chronology)

source_says: At the Kiowa sun dance — Summer 1845: sun dance on Kiowa Medicine-lodge creek
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), p. 228 (the Apache “have formed an integral part of the Kiowa tribal circle”) and calendar entry

source_says: Summer 1845: sun dance on Kiowa Medicine-lodge creek
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), calendar entry

source_says: Driven from Big Village by the Sioux in 1845, “this time permanently”, the Omaha move to a site west of the agency at Bellevue, near the mouth of the Platte, where they stay until the treaty of 1854
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Liberty, Wood, and Irwin, “Omaha”, p. 401

source_says: 1840–48: Rundle travels each summer along the foothills from Rocky Mountain House to the Bow River, preaching to the Stoney (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Getty and Gooding, “Stoney”, pp. 596–97

source_says: the fifth Day after levin Austin i found them incamped on the San Saba this was Mopechucope Band (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 262

source_says: Buffalo Hump and Pah hah yu co vilag air on the Clear Fork of the Brazos which they will rmane thair untl wee can get thir (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 262

source_says: Sept. 1845, Abert: the “Buffalo eaters” of “old Bald-Head”, “100 lodges or 200 men”, camped near Bent’s post on the Canadian (35°47′56″ N, 101°35′47″ W)
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), pp. 311–12 and n. 4

source_says: On the 12th Inst we met the Comanche Indians under Mo-pe-chu-co-pe, and encamped with them at the Council Ground near the Brazos River, and within four miles of this Post. In a day or two representatives from the Anadarko, Caddo, Cherokee, Delaware, Ioni, Lipan and Tonkawa, arrived (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 300

source_says: Mopechucope started in quest of Pah-hah yuco, and struck his trail high up the country and followed on it for several days, but was unable to overtake them ... Pah-hah yuco has gone a long way off, up among the Mountains and they do not think he will return this fall (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 364

source_says: by the 13th the Chiefs of Waco, Tawakoni, Keechi and Wichita, together with a number of their warriors, women and children, were upon the ground (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. Nos. 367-371

source_says: Report of a Council held with the Comanche Indians ... Mopechucope Ahkatsica, Santa Anna, ... who are all with exception of the first two, chiefs or captains belonging to Santa Anna's party. There was also present nearly Forty warriours (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 376

source_says: The Lipan have been removed from the San Antonio River to the San Gabriel above this place—The Tonkawa are on the Rio Blanco
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 386

source_says: The Tonkawa are on the Rio Blanco
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 2 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 386

source_says: Butler and Lewis 1846: the “Hooish” (Hois, the Penateka) “about 400 lodges, averaging about seven to the lodge making about 2800 souls”, probably on Neighbors’s information; “the only pre-epidemic count … it is unreliable”
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), pp. 299, 332, 385

source_says: Butler and Lewis, final report, July 1846: Yamparika 500 lodges and 3,500 souls; Hois 400 and 2,800; Kotsoteka over 300 and 2,000; Noonah 250 and 2,750; Nokoni 250 and 1,750; Tenewa 400 and 2,800 (sum 15,600; Butler’s March letter had five bands of about 500 lodges at 5 a lodge, 12,500). Kavanagh calls the list confused and the figures unreliable; the Handbook gives 14,300
source: Kavanagh, Comanche Political History: An Ethnohistorical Perspective, 1706–1875 (1996), pp. 297–99

source_says: 400 tipis, 2,000 souls (Bent)
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), “Population”

source_says: Bent: 2,000
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Brown and Irwin, “Ponca”, p. 430, table 1, citing Bent

source_says: the Lipan and Tonkawa are in much the same position, as regards locality, as they were at my last report. They are contented to occupy the vacant country between the San Marks [Marcos] and San Antonio Rivers
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 21

source_says: The two tribes has been invited to attend a council to be held at the Comanche Peak by Col. Butler and Majr. Lewis U. S. Commissioners on the part of the U. States and are now on their way to meet them. (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 21

source_says: The Lipan are also anxious to be settled and will plant corn and grain, this year on the Cibolo at their old Town. (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 21

source_says: Articles of a treaty made and concluded at Council Springs, in the county of Robertson Texas, near the Brazos River, this 15th day of May, A.D. 1846 ... Comanche, Ioni, Anadarko, Caddo, Lipan, Longwa, Keechi, Tah-wa-carro [Tawakoni], Wichita, and Waco (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. Nos. 59-60

source_says: Butler and Davis, 1846: Comanche or Na-u-ni, 14,300 (as tabulated by Schoolcraft beside Burnet 1847 and Neighbors 1849)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 100, table (Schoolcraft vol. 1, p. 518)

source_says: Butler and Davis, 1846: Waco, Wichita and Tawakoni (associates), 300 (as tabulated by Schoolcraft)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 100, table (Schoolcraft vol. 1, p. 518)

source_says: Mid-June 1846: Old Smoke’s village, moving toward Fort Laramie, met on the plain west of Scott’s Bluff
source: Parkman, The Oregon Trail (1849), ch. 8

source_says: At the Kiowa sun dance — Summer 1846: sun dance on a small tributary of the North Canadian above Medicine-lodge creek
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), p. 228 (the Apache “have formed an integral part of the Kiowa tribal circle”) and calendar entry

source_says: Summer 1846: sun dance on a small tributary of the North Canadian above Medicine-lodge creek
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), calendar entry

source_says: 1846: on the Brazos, 100 miles north of Comanche Peak (P.M. Butler; place ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Kitsai”, p. 568

source_says: Early July 1846: The Whirlwind’s Oglala village, “150 tall lodges”, joins Parkman’s camp at a bend of Laramie Creek above Fort Laramie (camp site ours, within about 30 km)
source: Parkman, The Oregon Trail (1849), ch. 11

source_says: 1846: Charles Bent reports “about 100 lodges of 500 Jicarillas throughout New Mexico”
source: Ortiz, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 10: Southwest (1983), Tiller, “Jicarilla Apache”, p. 451

source_says: Cheyenne ... 1846 ... [Lodges] 18 ... Ca. 200 [horses] ... Cheyenne camp visited near Fort Bent ... Garrard, 1927, pp. 52, 55. (part)
source: Ewers, The Horse in Blackfoot Indian Culture (BAE Bulletin 159, 1955), p. 24 (pdf 48)

source_says: Nov. 1846: the Cheyenne village on the Arkansas near the mouth of the Purgatoire; the people “talked of moving to the ‘Big Timber,’ a few miles” off
source: Garrard, Wah-to-yah and the Taos Trail (1850), pp. 45–53

source_says: Winter 1846–47: winter camp on Elk creek, tributary of the North fork of Red river
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), calendar entry

source_says: Major Nabors [Neighbors] returned to this place a few days since from Torreys trading house where he met the friendly Comanche Chiefs and various other Indian Tribes (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 76

source_says: Camp “composed mostly of old men, women, and children” attacked by Yankton and Santee on 12 Dec. 1846 on the Missouri (Burt County); “all the other chiefs were on a buffalo hunt”; more than 80 killed
source: Fletcher & La Flesche, “The Omaha Tribe” (BAE 27th Annual Report, 1911), p. 100

source_says: Nokoni “said to number 1,750, in 250 lodges, evidently a gross exaggeration”
source: Hodge ed., Handbook of American Indians North of Mexico (BAE Bulletin 30, 1907–10), “Detsanayuka”, vol. 1, p. 388

source_says: “In 1847 the Kansas or Kaw Indians numbered 1,500”
source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1868 (retrospect), p. 21

source_says: 1847: the Lipan “raise about 200 warriors of their own band” (800–1,000 people)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Opler, “Lipan Apache”, p. 945

source_says: Matlock: 1,600
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Brown and Irwin, “Ponca”, p. 430, table 1, citing Matlock

source_says: J.B. Dunbar: 8,400
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 563, table 3, citing J.B. Dunbar

source_says: Winter 1846–47: the Cheyenne village at the “Big Timber”, “a strip of woods extending for several miles along the river… which the Indians consider their future home”
source: Garrard, Wah-to-yah and the Taos Trail (1850), p. 127

source_says: Meusebach council with the Penateka chiefs Buffalo Hump, Santa Anna and Old Owl on the lower San Saba, about 25 miles from the Colorado, 1–2 Mar. 1847
source: Wikipedia, “Meusebach–Comanche Treaty” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Village on Papillion Creek “about 8 miles west of the present town of Bellevue … built in 1847”; lived there until the 1854 sale
source: Fletcher & La Flesche, “The Omaha Tribe” (BAE 27th Annual Report, 1911), p. 100

source_says: the Crow Indians had massacred about 30 lodges of this same band two years previous on the banks of the Yellowstone (part)
source: Denig, “Indian Tribes of the Upper Missouri” (BAE 46th Annual Report, 1930), p. 438 (pdf 37)

source_says: Santa Anna the Comanche Indian Chief who lately left that section of country very suddenly & under suspicious circumstances with all the women & children of his tribe, has returned ... Capt Grumbles advised Santa Anna to take his people and move on near Torreys Trading house on the Brassos river (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 5 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 27

source_says: “They can now raise about 200 warriors of their own band” (the Lipan, apart from the Mescalero and “Seratick”)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 78 (Burnet to Schoolcraft, 1847)

source_says: There are about 150 warriors of this tribe—they have usually warred within the limits of our settlements.
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 78

source_says: The Waco are the most considerable of these bands, amounting probably to 150 warriors, it being understood among Indians that every adult male is a warrior. ... They live in a village on the Upper Brazos, and raise corn, beans, pumpkins, etc., and usually spend the winter months in hunting. (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 78

source_says: The other small parties, amounting to about fifty families each, live in villages, on the waters of the Trinity and Neches, and cultivate the ground to a small extent. (place ours) (part)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 78

source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 5 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 27

source_says: These Indians range promiscuously across our frontier, from Red River to the Rio Grande, during the greater portion of the year, and seek shelter during the winter in the uppor cross timbers of Texas, between the head waters of the Colorado River and the Wichita Mountains. (place ours)
source: Winfrey and Day, eds., The Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, 1825–1916, vol. 3 (1966; repr. 1995), doc. No. 87
